title: What happens if you declare final int x; and print it without initializing it (compile error)?
shortTitle: What happens if you declare final int x without initializing?

s1_definition.profdef: It is a compile-time error. A `final` local variable has no default value and must be definitely assigned before it is read, so attempting to print `x` before assigning it fails compilation with a message such as "variable x might not have been initialized". This is distinct from a non-final local, which also must be assigned before use, and from a `final` field, which must be assigned by the end of the constructor or static initializer rather than at declaration. The compiler enforces definite assignment analysis to guarantee a final variable is read only after exactly one assignment.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, think of a final variable as an official sealed form field that must be filled in exactly once and can never be changed afterward. If a clerk tries to photocopy and submit the form while that mandatory field is still blank, the bank's validation rejects it outright before processing. You cannot read a value that was never written, and because the field is final, there is no default placeholder the bank fills in for you. The submission is rejected at check-in time, which is like the compile error happening before the program ever runs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reading an uninitialized final local is a compile error — final locals have no default and must be definitely assigned before use.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** It is a compile-time error. A `final` local variable has no default value and must be definitely assigned before it is read, so attempting to print `x` before assigning it fails compilation with a message such as "variable x might not have been initialized". This is distinct from a non-final local, which also must be assigned before use, and from a `final` field, which must be assigned by the end of the constructor or static initializer rather than at declaration. The compiler enforces definite assignment analysis to guarantee a final variable is read only after exactly one assignment.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, think of a final variable as an official sealed form field that must be filled in exactly once and can never be changed afterward. If a clerk tries to photocopy and submit the form while that mandatory field is still blank, the bank's validation rejects it outright before processing. You cannot read a value that was never written, and because the field is final, there is no default placeholder the bank fills in for you. The submission is rejected at check-in time, which is like the compile error happening before the program ever runs.

**One line to remember:** Reading an uninitialized final local is a compile error — final locals have no default and must be definitely assigned before use.

sections.s2_technical:
Local variables in Java, whether final or not, do not receive default values. The compiler performs definite assignment analysis, which proves that every local variable is assigned a value on every path that reaches a read of that variable. If any path can reach the print statement without having assigned x, compilation fails.

For a final local specifically, two rules combine. First, like all locals, it must be definitely assigned before being read. Second, because it is final, it must be assigned exactly once. So `final int x;` followed by `System.out.println(x)` with no assignment in between is rejected, because x is read while possibly unassigned.

This is different from fields. A non-final instance field that is never explicitly assigned defaults to 0 for an int, so printing it is legal and prints 0. A final instance field has no default and must be assigned either at its declaration or in every constructor; if a constructor finishes without assigning a final field, that is a compile error. A final static field must be assigned at declaration or in a static initializer block.

A senior nuance is that a final local can be declared first and assigned later, as long as it is assigned exactly once before any read. For example `final int x; x = compute(); print(x);` is perfectly legal. This is called blank final and is useful when the value depends on a branch, such as assigning different values in the two arms of an if-else, provided every path assigns exactly once. Another nuance is that definite assignment is a flow analysis, so the compiler can reject code even when a human can see a value would be assigned at runtime, because the rule is conservative and must hold on every possible path.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A developer at the National Bank declared a final fee variable intending to set it based on account type, but forgot to assign it on one branch and tried to use it. The build failed. This is exactly the compile error from reading a possibly-unassigned final local.

Problem 2 — The correct pattern is a blank final: declare the final fee once, then assign it exactly once in each branch of the decision, so every path assigns before use. This is exactly how a blank final is meant to be used.

Problem 3 — The team contrasts this with a final field that is assigned in the constructor, showing that a field has a different initialization rule than a local. This is exactly the field-versus-local distinction.

The code has a `FeePolicy` service that uses a blank final correctly, a commented-out broken version showing the compile error, and a `FinalInitDemo` main class, plus an `Account` with a final field assigned in the constructor.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a blank final int x, Rajesh's savings account SAV2001, and an account type of SAVINGS.

Step 1: The broken version declares final int x and immediately tries to print it. The compiler's definite assignment analysis finds a path that reads x without assigning it, so compilation fails before any code runs. There is no default value for a local, final or not.

Step 2: In the correct version, final int x is declared as a blank final and then assigned 20 exactly once. Now every path to the read has assigned x, so it compiles and prints 20.

Step 3: An Account is created. Its final fields are assigned inside the constructor. This is legal because a final field's rule is to be assigned by the end of the constructor, not necessarily at declaration.

Step 4: feeFor is called with type SAVINGS. The blank final fee is declared, and because the type is SAVINGS the if-branch assigns 100 rupees. The else branch would have assigned 250, so every path assigns fee exactly once.

Step 5: Because fee is definitely assigned on every path, the return statement reading fee is legal, and the fee of 100 rupees is returned.

Step 6: The fee is logged. The whole demo shows that the error is purely a compile-time check, and that blank finals are the correct way to assign a final after declaration.

```text
INFO: x after blank-final assignment = 20
INFO: Fee for SAV2001 = Rs.100.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  final int x;           (blank final, no value yet)
    │
    ├─ BROKEN: print(x) before assign ──→ COMPILE ERROR
    │           "variable x might not have been initialized"
    │
    └─ CORRECT: x = 20 (assign once) ──→ print(x) → 20

  FeePolicy.feeFor(account, "SAVINGS")
    final BigDecimal fee;          (blank final)
      ├─ type==SAVINGS → fee = 100.00 assigned
      └─ else          → fee = 250.00 assigned
    every path assigns exactly once → read fee → return Rs.100.00
```
sections.s5c_hld:

  ═══ HLD — Compile-Time Safety in the Build Pipeline ═══

  ┌────────────┐  push   ┌──────────────────┐  javac  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Developer  │───────→ │  CI Build Stage  │───────→ │  Artifact    │
  │ writes code│         │  (compile check) │         │  (jar)       │

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Initialization Rules by Kind ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              Initialization Matrix             │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ final LOCAL    : no default; must assign       │
  │                  before read (blank final OK)  │
  │ non-final LOCAL: no default; must assign        │
  │                  before read                   │
  │ final FIELD    : no default; assign at decl OR  │
  │                  in every constructor           │
  │ non-final FIELD: gets default (int→0) if unset  │
  │ final STATIC   : assign at decl OR in static {} │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  State of a blank final:
    [DECLARED] --assign once--> [ASSIGNED] --read--> OK
         │
         └── read while [DECLARED] → COMPILE ERROR
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
If I declare final int x and then try to print it without ever assigning it, the result is a compile-time error, with a message along the lines of variable x might not have been initialized. The program never even runs, because the error is caught by the compiler.

The reason is that local variables in Java, whether final or not, do not get default values. The compiler performs definite assignment analysis, which proves that every local is assigned on every path that reaches a read of it. If there is any path that reaches the print without assigning x, compilation fails. For a final local there is an extra rule layered on top: it must be assigned exactly once. So an uninitialized final that is read is rejected both because it was never assigned and because finals have no default placeholder.

It is important to distinguish this from fields. A non-final instance field defaults to zero for an int, so printing it is legal and prints zero. But a final field has no default and must be assigned either at its declaration or by the end of every constructor, otherwise that too is a compile error.

The correct and useful pattern is the blank final. I am allowed to declare final int x first and assign it later, as long as it is assigned exactly once before any read. This is very handy when the value depends on a branch. In our fee policy code, I declare a final fee variable, then assign it one value in the savings branch and another in the default branch, so every path assigns it exactly once, and only then do I read it. The compiler is satisfied because definite assignment holds on every path, and I get the safety guarantee that the fee is set exactly once and can never be accidentally changed afterward. This whole check happening at compile time means the bug is caught in our CI build and never reaches the running banking system.

---

keyPoints: Compile error if never assigned — blank final must be assigned exactly once
Instance blank final: must be set in every constructor
Static blank final: must be set in a static initializer block
Once assigned, cannot be changed — this is the "blank final" pattern
